title: Separatist party wins Quebec election, adding new test to Canada's unity
description: Canadian media projects the sovereigntist Parti Québécois (PQ) will secure a minority win in Monday's provincial election in Quebec, making Paul St-Pi
body: Canadian media projects the sovereigntist Parti Québécois (PQ) will secure a minority win in Monday's provincial election in Quebec, making Paul St-Pierre Plamondon the incoming premier.It marks the first time the PQ has been in power since 2014. It could prove to be a test for Prime Minister Mark Carney, setting up confrontations with Quebec over issues like immigration and the monarchy.The party has also pledged to hold a referendum on Quebec's independence, similar to an upcoming vote in province of Alberta later this month. The majority French-speaking province has held other votes on this, in 1980 and 1995. Polls indicate only 30% of Quebecers back such a move.Plamondon has said that vote would occur after US President Donald Trump is out of office.Carney may find himself managing dual unity crises in different parts of the country, depending on the outcome of the separation vote in Alberta. Trump is due to leave office in roughly two years, meaning that if Plamondon keeps his pledge, a third plebiscite on independence would likely be scheduled for 2029 or 2030. Separate from sovereignty, Plamondon has made it clear he is willing to fight Ottawa if it is seen as overstepping matters of provincial interest.He suggested during the campaign that he was going to pressure Ottawa, external on issues like immigration, vowing to fight any increases mandated by the Carney government.He also pledged to "abolish the monarchy in Quebec" and reroute money spent on its institutions to social services instead. "We are going to do what we have to do to get the monarchy out of Quebec, repatriate those funds, and send them to social causes," he told reporters in late September.For example, Plamondon suggested defunding Quebec's lieutenant-governor's office - responsible for representing King Charles III in the province - saying he would instead spend that money to tackle homelessness. Plamondon was among the Quebec lawmakers who refused to pledge allegiance to the King in 2022, paving the way for a provincial law that now makes the oath of allegiance optional.His plan to withdraw financial support for the lieutenant-governor's office is likely to face significant legal challenges, given the monarchy's central role in Canada's constitution.Such a move would also put future Quebec laws in doubt, as one of the key roles of the lieutenant-governor is to give royal assent to new legislation.Pressed about these hurdles, Plamondon has told reporters that he is ready for a legal battle with the federal government. The success of the Parti Québécois on Monday is in part due to public fatigue with the previous Coalition Avenir Québec government. Coalition Avenir Québec made safeguarding Quebec's identity and language central  to its eight years in office, but its longtime leader, François Legault, eventually lost significant support among voters. Efforts to revive the party by replacing Legault with a new leader, outgoing Premier Christine Fréchette, were unsuccessful.Fréchette conceded her own re-election race in Trois-Rivières shortly before 22:00 local time. She said in a speech that she would work with St-Pierre Plamondon on the transition. "Governing Quebec is the greatest honour I have ever had," she said. "I have Quebec tattooed on my heart." The Quebec Liberal Party secured the second-most seats, while the Quebec Conservative Party gained seats.Prime Minister Carney, who leads the federal Liberal party, remains popular in Quebec, though support for him had recently dipped, external as US President Donald Trump imposed new tariffs on Canada in August, following a breakdown in trade talks.Quebec is among the hardest hit by the latest US tariffs, with experts at global forecasting firm Oxford Economics projecting a C$2bn blow for the province. Carney congratulated Plamondon on his victory late on Monday and vowed to work together with the party. "Building a stronger Québec is core to our mission of building a stronger Canada," he said in a post on social media. "I look forward to working with you to support Québec's businesses and workers impacted by tariffs, create more good jobs, work to end homelessness, and get more homes built across Québec."

schema.headline: Separatist party wins Quebec election, adding new test to Canada's unity

title: 'Not again': Arrest of US marine for murder reignites protests in Japan's Okinawa
description: For many Okinawa locals, the arrest of a US soldier accused of robbing and killing a woman in a hotel room has reignited decades of frustration over c
body: For many Okinawa locals, the arrest of a US soldier accused of robbing and killing a woman in a hotel room has reignited decades of frustration over crimes involving US military personnel there."Honestly my first reaction was, 'Not again,'" 52-year-old longtime Okinawa resident Ai Sato told the BBC."Nothing has changed since I was a child. How many times are we going to repeat the same thing, create more victims, cause their families to suffer, and ultimately, cause the people of Okinawa to grieve?"Akemi Oshiro, a 62-year-old Ginowan resident shared similar sentiments."I know we shouldn't get used to terrible things like this, but because they keep happening, I've stopped being surprised,"  she told the BBC.Okinawa hosts the largest US military presence in Japan. It is home to several US military bases and tens of thousands of American troops.US Marine Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, was arrested by Japanese police on Sunday. Police say an investigation is underway and that Ballard is in Japanese custody because the alleged crime was unrelated to official military duties.Whether a US service member is acting in the performance of official duty, external or not can determine which country has primary jurisdiction. When Japan has jurisdiction, but the suspect is under US custody, they can retain custody until Japan brings charges.Ballard was assigned to III Marine Expeditionary Force and stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Ginowan City.The Okinawa prefectural police say 39-year-old Anna Yagi was found dead early 3 October in a hotel room in Naha.Security footage allegedly shows a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the woman and leaving alone with her belongings. Local media citing police have reported that Yagi appeared to have been strangled with a cord.Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi registered an official protest with Washington. But residents like Sato feel that's far from enough."I am deeply disappointed by the same kinds of government comments we have been hearing for decades -- that they will protest or that they take the matter seriously.""I want Prime Minister Takaichi to call President Trump directly, someone with whom she has been emphasizing as having a close relationship with, and discuss concrete measures to prevent this from happening yet again," she said.Following news of the suspected murder, people in Japan have been voicing anger with some 100 people protesting in both Naha and Tokyo. Others took to social media expressing their outrage and demanding justice with one user saying: "Enough is enough."Over the past few years, a number of accidents and crimes  have led to growing local opposition to the US presence on the island.The 2016 rape and murder of a 20-year-old local woman saw tens of thousands of protesters demonstrate against the heavy US presence there. A former US marine subsequently received a life sentence for the crime. The US currently has about 55,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, with the heaviest concentration based on the tropical island prefecture. Okinawa is one of the country's smallest prefectures by size, but 70% of the land used exclusively by the US military in Japan is located there.In 1972, Okinawa prefecture was returned to Japanese control after United States forces occupied the islands at the end of the Second World War. Since then, there have been 6,409 arrests for criminal offenses related to US military personnel, according to Okinawa Prefectural Government.Locals say the significant US presence has stirred resentment over a number of issues from crimes including rapes, assaults, and drunk-driving accidents to local disturbances such as noise and aircraft crashes.In 1995, three US servicemen abducted, beat, and raped a 12-year-old schoolgirl as she walked home from a stationery store.In 2025, a US Marine was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a Japanese woman."Even 80 yeas after the war, Okinawa where we live is a place that is so unnerving," 48-year-old mother of two boys Hitomi Miyagi told the BBC."We will not stop raising our voices hoping for an Okinawa, where we can live in peace."

schema.headline: 'Not again': Arrest of US marine for murder reignites protests in Japan's Okinawa

title: Trump says he will stop using US taxpayer funds for ads
description: There have been more than a dozen ads over recent weeks, with some mentioning  Trump's tax cuts, US manufacturing and law and order. In them, Trump al
body: There have been more than a dozen ads over recent weeks, with some mentioning  Trump's tax cuts, US manufacturing and law and order. In them, Trump also vows to take action against the "deep state" and others he perceives as enemies.In one ad, Trump says, "We will cast out the communists, Marxists, and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all".The ads come just ahead of the pivotal November midterm elections, when Democrats hope to take control of one or both chambers of the US Congress as polls continue to show Trump's approval rating falling. Midterm elections often serve as a verdict on how a president is doing - and typically the party of a sitting president tends to lose seats in Congress. The White House has pushed back against criticism, calling the ads "educational" and saying they are not propaganda, but rather public service announcements.They've pointed to previous administrations ads, like those under former Presidents Barack Obama on his healthcare plan and one under former President Joe Biden urging people to get Covid-19 vaccines.But legal experts say past US government adverts have typically been about public health or national emergencies."It's difficult to see what legitimate government purpose is served by spending taxpayer dollars on ads whose only apparent purpose is to promote the president," legal ethics expert Margaret Dylus-Yukins has told the BBC.Democratic Senator Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire introduced a measure, which was blocked by a Republican, denouncing the administration for using government funds for for the ads."It is the sense of the Senate that the advertisements promoting President Donald Trump that aired in September 2026, which included the direct language 'paid for by the U.S. Government,' should not be paid for by the United States government," the measure reads.The ads have received criticism on both sides of the aisle.Republican Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters on Monday that while "I like the message ... it shouldn't be paid for with taxpayer dollars".Senator John Kennedy, a Republican, said on CBS News on Sunday that politicians should not spend taxpayer funds on promotional ads."I don't think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves," the Louisiana lawmaker said.

schema.headline: Trump says he will stop using US taxpayer funds for ads

title: Anuv Jain: Rising Indian singer on new music and future hopes
description: Can you find success as an Indian artist, outside of the Bollywood machine, while making music that feels like you?Well according to Anuv Jain it's po
body: Can you find success as an Indian artist, outside of the Bollywood machine, while making music that feels like you?Well according to Anuv Jain it's possible - and you can even create something "beautiful". The singer-songwriter's soft vocals have gained hundreds of millions of views on YouTube - not an easy feat as an independent artist in India's music scene.BBC Newsbeat met Jain as he prepared for the final shows on the European leg of his first world tour to find out why he's taking his time and "hoping for the best". "It's not about the numbers," Jain tells us backstage, ahead of his sold-out performance at London's Roundhouse.But they do tell a story. Jain is from Ludhiana in the Punjab region of India and began singing as a teenager.His tracks have since racked up hundreds of millions of views on YouTube with their  emotional storylines about relationships and heartbreak.Jain primarily sings in Hindi, with his pieces often exploring deep emotions like love and longing. Fans talk about feeling like his music soundtracks their lives, external and is personal to them. His accessible style has attracted 3.9 million followers on Instagram and more than 20 million monthly listeners on Spotify.According to Jain, the secret to his success is simple.When writing music, he says, he imagines how someone listening in the car, going for a run or sitting alone at night would feel hearing the song."I just try to make a good song and something that I would like to listen to, something my mum, my sister and my wife would like to listen to," he says. "For some reason, the taste that we have in music is gentle enough that when we put it out there, there are millions of people who are wanting to consume all of this."Jain has attracted a sizeable fanbase without the backing of Bollywood, which has traditionally dominated the Indian music industry with opportunities and significant funding for artists.He's one of a growing number of independent musicians offering something different to the rollicking film scores and dramatic ballads that are synonymous with the country's movie industry.Jain describes artists like him as existing in an "alternate space"."We release music ourselves and hope for the best," he says.Jo Tum Mere Ho and Afsos, Jain's track with AP Dhillon, both reached number one on the Asian Music Charts, but the singer says there's no recipe to his success. Jain says he's "very selective" about the music he releases, only putting out one song a year until recently.But he plans to change that - and insists he has new songs coming "very soon". "They're done and I think they're beautiful songs so technically you might have more music this year," he says."It's not like it's gonna be just one release, let's see how it works out."The singer explains that seeing a project through is key - which might be why he limits what he puts out."There are no projects like right now for me that are half or that I haven't completed them yet. "When I start a project, I always finish it. I mean, I might have ideas, but as soon as I start writing, I finish it."Simplicity seems to do the trick, with certain passages , externalof Jain's songs, like Arz Kiya Hai, becoming hugely popular among his fanbase and going viral on TikTok and Instagram.There have been high-profile collaborations between some of western music and Indian music's biggest names in recent years. Jain says he'd be open to working with bigger stars, but only if his own identity can be preserved and things are done "the right way"."The storytelling cannot get diluted just because there's a bigger name attached," he says.But, he adds: "I'm not there yet". However, Jain does admit he could see himself joining forces with former One Direction star Zayn Malik, who's enjoyed success in both the Official Singles Chart and Official Asian Music Chart."He would be somebody who would definitely work very well with the kind of music that I make," says Jain."Maybe the universe will just make it happen."

schema.headline: Anuv Jain: Rising Indian singer on new music and future hopes

title: Donald Trump says a 'threat' led US to move bombers from RAF Fairford
description: Trump's comments appear to confirm reports by US media that a new threat led to the bombers being removed after a major incident on 27 September when
body: Trump's comments appear to confirm reports by US media that a new threat led to the bombers being removed after a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.While speaking to a gaggle of reporters outside the White House, Trump was asked if a "specific threat" had led the US to pull its bombers from the airbase.Trump replied: "Yeah I think we can say that. They didn't fly out by accident."There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy. But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far."He added Washington "actually knows the people that made the threat", but he did not confirm who.The exact nature of the threat that prompted the aircraft's removal from RAF Fairford remains unclear, but sources in Washington speculated to the BBC it might have revolved around sabotage attempts or attempts to strike the sensitive, expensive aircraft in the event of resumed hostilities with Iran.One source close to the White House pointed to Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb - a covert drone attack on five Russian bases in June last year - as an example of what an enemy force could do, even at a distance."Whatever they thought it was, it was taken extremely seriously," the source said.Trump's comments, and those of Vance before him, stand in stark contrast to those of Secretary of State Marco Rubio.While both Trump and Vance pointed to an unspecified threat, Rubio was much more guarded in his language, noting that it was "not unusual" for military units and assets to rotate and be moved around the world.RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - has been at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police.Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.Following the release of the first five men, Trump criticised the decision and US officials suggested Iran could have been involved in the incident.Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire.Speaking earlier on Monday, Rubio said he would not directly tie last week's incident to the decision to pull bombers from RAF Fairford.He added: "It's not unusual to see movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in and old planes going out."Rubio said the US still had full confidence in the security of all its bases and that British authorities had been very co-operative since the incident.Vance later said the bombers had been moved out of an "abundance of caution", adding Washington felt Iran was doing what it had "done for 49 years... which is engage in acts of terrorism against the US and against a lot of other people".Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but he did not provide further details, while Rubio said it had "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor" without going into further details.Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford, has been used as a forward operating location by the US air force for decades.In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.The redeployment from RAF Fairford will reduce America's capacity to "quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat", Christoph Bergs, research analyst at defence think tank the Royal United Services Institute told the Reuters news agency.However, the use of the base had already been limited given London's stipulation that it should only be used for defensive strikes, he added. The planes could potentially be sent to either Diego Garcia or bases in the Gulf to reduce the need for air-to-air refuelling but that would depend on capacity availability, negotiations with allies and security, Bergs added.

schema.headline: Donald Trump says a 'threat' led US to move bombers from RAF Fairford

title: US 'watching closely' after plague researcher dies in Russia
description: President Donald Trump says the US is looking "very strongly" at the case of a Russian lab technician who died at a plague research centre in Siberia.
body: President Donald Trump says the US is looking "very strongly" at the case of a Russian lab technician who died at a plague research centre in Siberia.Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was watching closely amid concerns the incident could lead to the spread of pneumonic plague, but there was no cause for alarm.Announcing the cause of death as "pneumonia of undetermined etiology", Irkutsk's governor said "no micro-organisms" linked to the woman's work had been found "in her biological samples".Unconfirmed reports suggested the woman fell ill either after breaking a test tube containing the pathogen or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents.Asked what Washington was going to do about the risk of plague spreading from Russia, Trump said he had not spoken to the Kremlin about it."I hate to see them having it," he said, but added: "We'll help. Everybody who has that kind of a problem, we'll always help."No other cases of staff from the plague institute seeking medical attention since the lab technician's death had been reported, Irkutsk governor Igor Kobzev said, quoting Russia's consumer and health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor.The watchdog said a biological safety team had inspected the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk and found no emergency situation there.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged people not to "listen to various rumours" but "rely on Rospotrebnadzor's official statements" instead.Russian media reported last week that nearly 200 people known to have had contact with the dead woman were under medical observation as a precaution.Asked by a reporter for an "update on the suspected plague case in Russia", Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: "It seems that there was a worker at the lab that was infected and there's concern that that, you know, could have spread, at least internally - you've seen them do quarantine of this and that nature. "If something like that gets out, it can quickly spread. So we're watching and monitoring it closely. I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and the cause to just keep an eye on it and we're doing that."The woman who died, whose first name was given by Russian media as Daria and who was in her late twenties, had recently visited the Buryatia region on the border with Mongolia.The plague bacterium or Yersinia pestis, external, which killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death, is found among rodents such as marmots in the area.  It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, external was founded just over 100 years ago.Dr Simon Clarke, an associate professor in cellular microbiology at the University of Reading, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the pneumonic version of Yersinia pestis was nearly always fatal if left untreated, but could be overcome with antibiotics.     "Pneumonic plague can transmit from person to person and that is why there is the concern around this," he said.    He added: "But of course people's thought with any outbreak of infectious disease at all runs to... lockdowns and Covid and that is just not what's going to happen here.""People think, 'Oh the plague, that's gone, that went hundreds of years ago,' but it hasn't," Clarke said. "It's still around and in certain parts of the world, it's a threat to human health and that's why they need to study it."Asked if the pathogen might have been studied for potential use as a bio-weapon, the scientist agreed it was possible."Because this is Russia people's thoughts are running to that, but I think my earlier explanation is probably more likely," Clarke said.

schema.headline: US 'watching closely' after plague researcher dies in Russia

title: Spain PM pins hopes on housing crisis to help win snap election
description: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's decision to call a snap election for 29 November came on the back of a parliamentary defeat. On Friday, the raf
body: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's decision to call a snap election for 29 November came on the back of a parliamentary defeat. On Friday, the raft of measures he had presented to congress aimed at improving conditions for tenants and trying to address the problem of soaring rentals was narrowly rejected, as parties on the right voted against them.That parliamentary result confirmed that Sánchez's left-wing coalition no longer commanded a majority. But as has so often been the case throughout Sánchez's career, the calling of the election was not a knee-jerk reaction but a carefully thought-out manouevre.His government has been struggling in recent months. His Socialist Party has been mired in corruption, with cases implicating former senior figures in the party, Santos Cerdán and José Luis Ábalos, while the former Socialist Prime Minister, José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, is facing accusations of having benefited financially from the government's bailout of an airline. Zapatero has denied wrongdoing.In addition, Sánchez's wife, Begoña Gómez, is due to go on trial over allegations of misuse of funds and influence peddling - accusations that Gómez and Sánchez vehemently deny.Meanwhile, Sánchez's administration has struggled to manage the crisis in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in North Africa, where more than 70,000 migrants suddenly arrived in July. Most have returned over the border to Morocco, but the city has become a political and logistical headache for the prime minister.The PP and Vox tend to oppose any initiative presented by the Sánchez government, which they have long cast as illegitimate due to its scandals and reliance on Catalan and Basque nationalists. However, as a matter of policy, parties on the right tend to oppose the kind of direct intervention in the housing market that Sánchez has been advocating, warning that it can be counterproductive.Earlier this year, when Sánchez's international profile rose due to his outspoken criticism of Israel's actions in Gaza and his clashes with US President Donald Trump, there was speculation that he might have used the political capital that gave him on the left and called an early election back then. However, the housing issue, which is the biggest concern for Spaniards according to polls, appears more likely to mobilise support on the left.Yet polls also show that the Socialists are trailing the PP. While the housing issue provides Sánchez with a potential fillip on the campaign trail, staying in power after these elections will be probably the biggest challenge of his career.

schema.headline: Spain PM pins hopes on housing crisis to help win snap election

title: Yemeni military says it has retaken Mokha and 'secured' Red Sea waterway
description: Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia say they have "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, at the start
body: Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia say they have "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, at the start of a major offensive against the Iran-backed Houthi movement.The Yemeni military also said in a statement that National Shield, Giants Brigades and Tihama Resistance forces had captured the Red Sea city of Mokha on Monday afternoon with the help of Saudi air strikes. But in conflicting reports, unnamed Yemeni government and military sources told news agencies Reuters and AFP that the forces have only reached the city's outskirts.The Houthis said they had struck Riyadh's international airport on Monday, but have not commented regarding Mokha.Four government sources told Reuters that Yemeni forces had reached the outskirts of Mokha late on Monday, and that Houthi fighters were now retreating.Government military sources who spoke to AFP would not confirm the capture of the city, but said "our forces took control of the Dhubab military airfield and cut the road linking the Dhubab district to the Bab al-Mandab area".Earlier, the Yemeni military also said its forces had seized Dhubab airport, 45km (27 miles) to the south, and were besieging Houthi fighters inside the nearby town.Houthi-run media denied reports that government forces had also made advances in Dhubab.The government said operations had also begun on other fronts on Monday, including the capital Sanaa, which fell to the Houthis at the start of the civil war 12 years ago.Meanwhile, a Saudi-led military coalition said its fighter jets were providing "round-the-clock" air support to the pro-government forces and had destroyed 324 "high-value" targets since the start of the offensive.Turkey and Pakistan, allies of Saudi Arabia, held an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday and agreed to rapidly deploy military forces in Saudi Arabia in an invocation of their Mecca defence pact, according to a joint statement shared by Pakistan's foreign ministry.Saudi air strikes killed a schoolgirl and a woman in the Sanhan and Saawan districts of Sanaa on Monday, according to Houthi-run Al Masirah TV.Houthi spokesman Mohammed Abdul Salam said Saudi Arabia was committing "dozens of massacres" and that it must "bear all the consequences".The Houthi-run Humanitarian Operations Co-ordination Centre warned civilian airlines that Saudi airspace, except for the skies above the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina, was no longer safe because it had become "a theatre of operations".UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres condemned "the continued Houthi cross-border attacks" on Saudi Arabia and said he was "deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting", in a statement to AFP.On Sunday, the head of Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council announced the beginning of an offensive, dubbed Operation Yemen Dawn, aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.Rashad al-Alimi insisted that all opportunities for de-escalation had been exhausted and called on all forces to carry out their assigned missions "until the country is liberated from the grip of the Houthi terrorist militia".It came after the Houthis reportedly cut a mountain road near the south-western city of Taiz, effectively leaving government forces and residents there surrounded.The Houthis also said they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at oil facilities belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia in retaliation for dozens of Saudi strikes on their territory.In addition to the strikes on Riyadh's international airport, the Houthis attacked an Aramco oil refinery, and Abha airport, as well as other sites, according to Yemen's Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree in a statement on Telegram.According to BBC Verify, satellite imagery from Saturday shows thick, dark smoke coming from the site of a strike at the Aramco Riyadh Refinery, in the city's south-east.A similar plume of smoke can be seen rising from the Khurais Central Processing Facility as well as from a potential strike point in satellite imagery from Sunday.Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and quickly ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including Mokha, Dhubab and Perim (Mayyun) Island.They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.At least 959 people have been killed and 5,000 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry.The UN says another 197,000 people have been displaced.

schema.headline: Yemeni military says it has retaken Mokha and 'secured' Red Sea waterway

title: Trade: How India became dangerously addicted to Chinese imports
description: Take a walk into an Indian toy shop and as well as picking up a new favourite plaything for a child, you might just get an insight into how the nation
body: Take a walk into an Indian toy shop and as well as picking up a new favourite plaything for a child, you might just get an insight into how the nation is battling for a better economic relationship with its all-powerful neighbour China.Six years ago, in an attempt to push local manufacturing and keep substandard toys out of its market, India raised tariffs on imported toys from 20% to 60% and eventually to 70%.Retailers were up in arms and said that domestic firms could never match the foreign-made stuff. But the combination of higher customs duties and quality control standards worked.Indian imports of toys fell by a third from nearly $300m (£227m) in 2020 to $100m this year, while exports rose from around $129m to $200m in the same period. Moreover, the country was able to drastically reduce its dependence on China, which held a 70% share of the local toy market.The sector stands out as a rare exception in India's otherwise unsuccessful attempts to rebalance an increasingly lopsided trading relationship with its larger neighbour, which some experts say, is now among the most asymmetric in the world.Even as diplomatic ties between the two countries completely broke down following the Galwan Valley clashes in 2020 and Delhi announced a slew of anti-dumping duties and a ban on Chinese apps such as Tik Tok, its trade deficit with Beijing has only ballooned - from $44bn in 2020 to an eye-popping $112bn this year."India's economic dependence on China continued to deepen while political, security, and investment ties were at their lowest point," Kevin Zongzhe Li, a Washington-based Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Centre for China Analysis, told the BBC.More worryingly, exports to China remained below pre-pandemic level even as imports doubled in this period."China now supplies over 30% of India's industrial imports, and India depends on it for more than 100 critical products. And the imbalance is worsening," says Ajay Srivastava of the Delhi-based Global Trade and Research Initiative (GTRI).If the rapid pace of imports continues, bilateral deficit could jump to $134bn, giving Beijing even more leverage over Indian industry, according to Srivastava.On the sidelines of the Brics summit in Delhi in September, amid a deepening thaw between the Asian giants, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping vowed to address, external these "structural trade imbalances and supply chain issues".But given how deeply entrenched Chinese imports have become to India's industrial economy, this will be a formidable task for Delhi, experts told the BBC.That's primarily because India depends on China to not merely consume end-products, but increasingly to produce industrial goods.To be true, India has reduced its reliance on imports of finished goods such as smartphones and solar equipment, and now produces more than a quarter of the world's iPhones."Yet, production remains largely assembly-based and depends heavily on imported components, particularly from China," says Srivastava.It's the same story with industrial machinery, battery inputs, chemicals, solar cells, and manufacturing equipment.Electrical machinery and electronics alone account for 36% of imports, followed by machinery and mechanical appliances at 21.7%, while organic chemicals and plastics also have a significant share, according to the Observer Research Foundation (ORF) think tank."Their interruption would not merely affect consumption; it would disrupt production itself," according to Soumya Bhowmik, a Fellow at ORF's Centre for New Economic Diplomacy, who argues that this reflects India's difficulty in substituting Chinese inputs with local production.Besides a growing reliance on inputs and raw material, Chinese imports to India are also being propelled by other macroeconomic trends.China has huge excess capacity in sectors from steel to solar panels and electric vehicles, while its slowing economy cannot absorb the output.Manufacturers are therefore increasingly turning to overseas markets, selling goods cheaply. China's trade surplus is expected to top $1tn for a second straight year.A lot of these goods are coming to Indian shores because it is rapidly expanding manufacturing across segments of the economy, but also as "Western markets impose tariffs and other restrictions", says Srivastava.On the other hand, lack of access to the Chinese market remains a major challenge for Indian companies."Indian products face a variety of tariff and non-tariff hurdles in China that make it difficult to scale exports," says Li."If normalisation [of ties] continues without a serious push for reciprocal market access, India risks a situation where the political relationship improves but the economic dependency stays the same."The long term solution to both reducing avoidable imports and improving exports performance will be to strengthen manufacturing, says Srivastava.But that requires sector-specific industrial policy and stronger fundamentals – affordable power and credit, efficient logistics and stable regulations – areas where India still falls short.India has also recently softened foreign direct investment rules, which could open the door to Chinese companies wanting to expand Indian investments. But these too will need careful vetting, he adds."Investment that merely expands distribution networks or assembles products using Chinese parts could increase imports and deepen dependence. Approvals should therefore prioritise technology transfer, local value addition, domestic component production and exports from India."More immediately, India could focus on targeting higher exports to China in specific sectors to reduce its trade asymmetry, says Li. Sectors like pharmaceuticals could be a natural fit with China's population aging and healthcare costs rising."But narrowing a $112bn deficit won't come from finding niche export sectors alone," he adds."The key question is whether Beijing is ready and willing to make concessions on market access as part of the broader normalisation. Alternatively, India will need to find its own leverage to force that conversation."Follow BBC News India on Instagram, external, YouTube,, external X, external and Facebook, external.

schema.headline: Trade: How India became dangerously addicted to Chinese imports

title: MPs call for investigation after Howard  Lutnick-Jeffrey Epstein whistleblower dies
description: In July, Andriesz told MPs and campaigners the FCA had been fully informed about other serious allegations he had made as long ago as 2018 and accused
body: In July, Andriesz told MPs and campaigners the FCA had been fully informed about other serious allegations he had made as long ago as 2018 and accused it of inaction.The FCA told the BBC in July it had acted on his allegations and pointed to a supervision order it had issued based on his information.But in Andriesz's view that amounted to little more than a regulatory "slap on the wrist" and made it harder to make a claim for whistleblower retaliation against BGC at tribunal.Later that month, he told a meeting of the campaign group the Transparency Task Force the FCA was not fulfilling its obligations to the public and whistleblowers and merely "pays lip service" to the rules and regulations."It protects the institution and then exposes the whistleblower to extreme retaliation and devastation to their lives and families," he said.The FCA told the BBC it was appointing a new non-executive director on its board, former Bank of England director Lea Paterson, to conduct a review into Andriesz's treatment and the FCA's handling of his whistleblower allegations.An FCA spokesperson said: "We are very sorry to hear of Mr Andriesz's death. Our thoughts are with his family and friends."Since expressing our condolences, we'd asked Lea Paterson, who has just joined our board as a non-executive director, to review how we interacted with Mr Andriesz to learn any lessons for the future."

title: Nifty: Five reasons India's markets are sinking even when its economy is growing
description: India's economy is growing at an enviable rate of over 7% despite global energy shocks, rising interest rates, tariff uncertainties and weather-relate
body: India's economy is growing at an enviable rate of over 7% despite global energy shocks, rising interest rates, tariff uncertainties and weather-related disruptions.But the world's fastest growing major economy also has one of the worst performing major equity markets in 2026. The correction in Indian stocks has, in fact, only intensified in recent weeks.The benchmark Sensex and Nifty indices, which represent the country's largest companies, have inched up slightly since Monday after posting losses for eight straight weeks - the longest losing streak in 25 years, according to Reuters.Indian mom-and-pop investors who put their money into the Nifty have seen their wealth erode by about 15% this year. In comparison, they would have made 62% returns on Korea's Kospi index since January or 170% in the last two years.On aggregate, the money foreign investors have put into Indian markets in the past decade - after subtracting what they sold or withdrew - is nearing zero. In the past two years alone, foreign institutional investors have withdrawn a staggering $40bn, according to data from Bernstein Research.It is the large pool of domestic institutional and retail money, flowing into instruments like mutual funds, that have helped the markets avoid a sharper fall.Domestic assets under management of mutual funds have grown from about $125bn in 2016 to some $900bn this year, with the number of Indians parking money in stocks and mutual funds more than tripling to 150 million individuals.This makes the recent fall in the markets more worrying - since households, already struggling from a weak job market, high inflation and faltering consumption, are now seeing their equity savings take a beating too.So, what's gone wrong? Here are five reasons India's booming economy isn't lifting its stock market.Crude oil prices have hovered between $90 and $100 a barrel as the disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz enters its eighth month, far longer than analysts had expected. Moreover, there's little visibility on when normalcy will return."This single variable tends to influence the markets quite negatively," Hari Shyamsunder, a fund manager with Franklin Templeton Asset Management India, told the BBC. "Markets can absorb crude between $70 and $90, but when prices move above $100 a barrel, it starts putting stress on macro-economic variables such as inflation and also company earnings and margins." India imports over 90% of its requirements - nearly half of its crude oil imports, along with a large share of its liquified petroleum gas (LPG) and liquified natural gas (LNG) shipments, come through the Strait of Hormuz.While Delhi has diversified its energy sources, tapping Russian oil markets, US President Donald Trump recently threatened up to 100% tariffs on countries doing trade with Moscow, further complicating matters.In India, AI, or the new economy broadly, is a major missing piece of its growth story."Many of India's large caps [big companies] represent a bygone economic era," Bernstein Research said in a note recently. "Most are not investing in the future, but consolidating their past, often expecting policy to continue shielding them from global competition."India seeks AI breakthrough - but is it falling behind?And its smaller companies are yet to reach a scale that will attract foreign institutional funds.While Indian companies are investing in data centres and chip fabrication, the country has not produced a global giant like OpenAI, Anthropic or even China's DeepSeek - this is where the largest share of the profits in the AI value chain lie.Foreign investor interest will only return to India meaningfully if it can build globally competitive industries in these emerging areas, according to Bernstein."We are seeing early signs of this in areas such as space, defence, semiconductors, and deep-tech innovation, but most remain too small to materially influence capital allocation decisions over much of this decade."

schema.headline: Nifty: Five reasons India's markets are sinking even when its economy is growing

title: Saudi Arabia urged to spare Sri Lankan sentenced to death over Facebook post
description: "I plead for mercy for the wrongs committed by my son. Please forgive him and send him back to us."Speaking through tears, Rasamanickam Yogalakshmi ma
body: "I plead for mercy for the wrongs committed by my son. Please forgive him and send him back to us."Speaking through tears, Rasamanickam Yogalakshmi made a desperate plea for the life of her eldest son, Anojan Sivarasa. The 24-year-old migrant worker is facing the death penalty in Saudi Arabia after an appellate court found him guilty of blasphemy against Islam and the Prophet Muhammad over a comment he made on Facebook.The case has sent shockwaves through Sri Lanka, sparking widespread concern and civil society petitions across the country. Multiple political parties and government bodies have co-ordinated diplomatic efforts seeking clemency.However, the family has had no updates on his condition since 28 September. The Sri Lankan government has instructed the family to refrain from making further statements while diplomatic efforts take place.Saudi authorities have not published an official execution timeline, and it remains unclear when the sentence will be carried out. Saudi Arabia has a history of carrying out executions without warning families or foreign embassies, only informing relatives after the sentence has been carried out.Anojan was prosecuted after a dispute on social media following an incident that took place during a Hindu pilgrimage in Sri Lanka. In late June, footage of a young Muslim man kicking a dog following Hindu pilgrims circulated widely on social media, triggering religious arguments online.During the exchange, a user posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity, leading Anojan to post a response in Tamil insulting the Prophet Muhammad.Although Anojan promptly deleted his comment and posted an apology video, it was screenshotted and brought to the attention of his employer and Saudi officials, leading to his arrest in July.His personal devices were subsequently seized, and his social media accounts were deleted by Saudi officials."People in Saudi Arabia knew nothing about this matter. It was individuals in Sri Lanka who sent emails to the company where my brother worked. I do not even wish to mention who those people are," Anojan's brother, Hamsidan Sivarasa, told BBC Sinhala.The company employing Anojan notified the authorities in Saudi Arabia who registered a case against him, according to Hamsidan.Anojan was initially sentenced to five years in prison as well as a fine of 3m Saudi riyals (about $0.8m; £0.6m) by the Al-Ahsa Criminal Court. An appeal submitted on Anojan's behalf seeking to reduce his sentence was rejected, according to Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath.The case took a drastic turn on 17 September after Saudi prosecutors filed an appeal for Anojan to be prosecuted under Sharia law instead of the country's cybercrime legislation. The appellate court granted the prosecution's request, increasing his sentence to the death penalty.The Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Sri Lanka confirmed it is taking all available steps to assist Anojan.His family met President Anura Kumara Dissanayake at the Presidential Secretariat on 21 September. The president assured them that the government would spare no effort to obtain a general pardon for him, instructing diplomatic channels to engage Saudi authorities.The case has brought together cross-religious support. Senior Buddhist leaders, the Mahanayake Theros of the Ramanna Nikaya and the Amarapura Maha Nikaya, together with Hindu religious leaders, handed over a memorandum to the Presidential Secretariat calling for urgent state intervention.In addition, a four-member Sri Lankan legal delegation is travelling to Saudi Arabia this week to meet Anojan's local defence lawyers. "There are two law firms in Saudi Arabia handling Anojan's case. We are going there to meet the lawyers from these two firms, discuss the case and plan what can be done next," one of the team, Upul Kumarapperuma, President's Counsel, told BBC Sinhala.Back home, communication between Anojan and his family has completely ceased. "My brother hasn't called for two days." Hamsidan said on 28 September. "We informed the embassy and asked officials to look into the matter and update us. They said they would check. We are still waiting, as we have not yet received a response."In Saudi prisons, inmates on death row typically lose access to personal mobile devices, with formal calls strictly facilitated through prison authorities.Human rights organisations have repeatedly raised concerns regarding severe sentences for online speech in Saudi Arabia.In July 2023, Mohammed Al Ghamdi, a retired Saudi school teacher, was sentenced to death over his comments on multiple social media platforms, according to the United Nations."The death sentence against Mohammad bin Nasser al-Ghamdi, who has a total of just 10 followers on both of his anonymous Twitter accounts and is accused of nothing other than expressing his opinions on social media, is ludicrous," Philip Luther, Amnesty International's Research and Advocacy Director for the Middle East and North Africa, said at the time.Al Ghamdi's ruling was overturned, and he was sentenced to 30 years in prison, according to ALQST for human rights, an independent non-governmental organisation defending and promoting human rights in Saudi Arabia.There are more than 10 million foreign workers in Saudi Arabia, according to the International Organisation for Migration (IOM). Rights groups emphasise that low-wage migrant workers face distinct vulnerabilities in the Saudi legal system due to language barriers and lack of proper legal representation.Executions for blasphemy are relatively rare compared with those for drug offences or murder handed down by courts in Saudi Arabia.

title: A simple guide to the US midterms
description: ByJames FitzGeraldThere are four weeks to go until the US midterm elections, when voters take part in a ballot that could have a major impact on the r
body: ByJames FitzGeraldThere are four weeks to go until the US midterm elections, when voters take part in a ballot that could have a major impact on the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.What are the midterms?On 3 November, Americans will choose members of Congress, which is made up of two parts - the House of Representatives and the Senate.Elections take place every two years, and when they happen in the middle of the president's four-year term of office, they are called the midterms.A key task of Congress is to create and pass federal laws - laws that apply nationwide.The outcome of the midterms will decide which political party - Trump's Republicans or opposition Democrats - controls Congress and how easy it is for the president to carry out his plans.The results are also seen as a measure of how happy people in the US are with the president's performance so far.Who is being elected?All 435 members of the House - the lower chamber of Congress - will be elected. They serve fixed terms of two years. The House is where proposed laws are introduced and debated.Meanwhile, 35 of 100 seats in the Senate, the upper chamber, will also be up for grabs. Senators serve six-year terms. Among other jobs, they approve or block proposed laws that have been received from the House.On the same day, voters across much of the US will also choose state-level politicians. Governor contests in California, Florida, Georgia and Michigan will be among the most closely watched.What are the key issues?The US economy is on the minds of many voters struggling with the price of fuel, groceries, housing and healthcare.Inflation remains above the level targeted by the US Federal Reserve, partly down to the war that the US and Israel started with Iran in February.Democrats argue Trump's programme of trade tariffs have also pushed up prices for Americans.Immigration is another key issue. Republicans say Trump has delivered on a major campaign pledge in 2024 by tightening the border and launching a widespread - and often controversial - crackdown on illegal immigration.Concerns over AI have grown in urgency in recent weeks. Senior politicians from both parties have agreed on the need to regulate it - setting themselves in opposition to Trump, who has rejected the idea of laws to control development of the technology. What is at stake?Congress is one of the three branches of government, alongside the presidency and the judiciary. Control of it matters for the shaping of legislation.Both the House and Senate are currently held by the Republican Party. But its majority is a slender one. They have 218 seats in the House, which is the minimum number needed to control it, plus one independent who votes with them. In the Senate, they have 53 seats and the minimum needed for control is 51.If opposition Democrats win back control of at least one chamber, they will gain power to bring their own laws to the floor.Who might win?Voters have tended to "punish" the party of the president in the past and vote against them.Recent polling shows a low approval rating for the president. He began his second term as president with an approval rating of just over 50%, according to polling resource website Silver Bulletin, but in early October it was sitting at about 37%. Meanwhile 61% disapproved of him.But not all seats in each chamber are competitive. Some are a safe bet for Republicans or Democrats.The BBC's US partner CBS News has identified nine Senate races to watch, external, in states like Iowa and New Hampshire, and 42 House races, in states like Arizona and Ohio.The vote is more unpredictable this year because of a battle between the two parties over the way voting districts in the House of Representatives are drawn.Republicans tried to gain an advantage by creating more favourable electoral maps in certain states and Democrats followed suit.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Josh Turek (Democrat) and Ashley Hinson (Republican) are in a tight race for Iowa's Senate seatWhat does it mean for Trump?If the Democrats win either the House or the Senate then Trump will find it difficult to get any laws through Congress.So his domestic plans could be frustrated, although he has found ways to exercise power without his wider party.Democratic control of either chamber would also mean they could use committees to investigate aspects of the Trump presidency. Corruption allegations, the new White House ballroom and ICE tactics could be subject to scrutiny.There is also a debate within the Democratic Party about whether to impeach Trump, which means to bring charges in Congress that will form the basis for a political, not criminal, trial.If the Republican Party stays in control of Congress, Trump will be able to keep going with his plans for the remainder of his time in office.What does it mean for the 2028 election?The president's name is not on the ballot during the midterm elections, though Trump has urged Republicans to pretend that it is by voting for him as an endorsement of his actions so far.Whichever way the results fall, commentators are likely to use them to make arguments about how voters feel about the direction of the country under Trump's leadership.Trump cannot run to be president a third time. After the midterms, we can expect speculation to start building about who might be his successor as the Republican presidential nominee for 2028 - and who might compete against that person for the Democrats.

schema.headline: A simple guide to the US midterms

title: Brazil election goes to run-off as right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro wins first round
description: Right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro has won the first round of Brazil's presidential election, beating left-wing President Lula da Silva, but falling short of
body: Right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro has won the first round of Brazil's presidential election, beating left-wing President Lula da Silva, but falling short of an outright majority.There will be a run-off between the two candidates on 25 October.Bolsonaro is the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence for masterminding a failed coup after losing the 2022 election.Sunday's vote was close, with President Lula polling slightly ahead during the campaign. With almost all of the votes counted, Bolsonaro has 47% to Lula's 45% of the vote.Bolsonaro's result exceeded expectations, meaning the second round now looks like his to lose, given some of the other candidates knocked out in the first round were right-wing alternatives.His Liberal Party (PL) also had the most governors, senators and federal deputies elected in the results so far, meaning the party is expected to have the most influence in Congress.The majority of Latin America has now elected right-wing presidents, aligned to the Trump administration, and the run-off will determine whether Brazil – Latin America's largest country and economy – will follow suit.Speaking to reporters at the White House, US President Donald Trump said he expected the election to be "very close", but that Bolsonaro has had a "very, very big victory" in the first round.After casting his ballot, Lula, 80, warned the choice was between democracy and "barbarism".Bolsonaro, 45, said he wanted to "free the Brazilian people".Lula and Bolsonaro are the two biggest names in Brazilian politics, on the left and right, and this campaign has polarised Brazil yet again: with themes of sovereignty, crime, the economy and corruption being top concerns for voters.Lula is more popular in Brazil's poorer northeast, among low-income voters, Catholics, and women.He is seeking a fourth term in office, after being elected in 2002, 2006 and then a later non-consecutive term in 2022. In that election, he beat Jair Bolsonaro by less than 2% of the vote, the closest presidential election result in Brazil's history.After that election, Bolsonaro's supporters vandalised government buildings on 8 January 2023.Jair Bolsonaro was banned from running for re-election even before his prison sentence, but endorsed his eldest son Flávio to run in his place. Jair Bolsonaro's wife, Michelle, was elected to the Senate on Sunday.Flávio Bolsonaro has pledged to grant his father, and his supporters responsible for the 8 January riots, amnesty if elected.He is more popular in the south, and among wealthier voters and evangelical Christians.Bolsonaro said on Sunday he was "very happy" to have led Lula in the first-round vote, and expressed confidence that he would clinch a run-off victory in three weeks' time."I am very happy with the real possibility that, three weeks from now, Brazil will give a definitive answer by choosing a modern government," he said, according to AFP.Lula said the outcome of the vote was "unexpected", but insisted the race was not over."I admit I was convinced I would win in the first round," he said on Sunday. "The game is about to start. We are in extra time. In extra time, we will win over the Brazilian people."Corruption became a key issue in this campaign after a scandal involving a jailed banker, Daniel Vorcaro, who orchestrated one of Brazil's largest financial frauds, embroiling senior figures across the political spectrum.Bolsonaro acknowledged that he'd asked Vorcaro to bankroll a biopic about his father after voice recordings emerged in which he could be heard asking for 134 million reais ($25.9m; £19.5m).Lula was also impacted by the scandal indirectly, after police suggested Vorcaro had reached out to the Supreme Court judge Alexandre de Moraes to ask for help avoiding arrest. Moraes denies any wrongdoing.Moraes was not appointed by Lula but is seen as his ally, given Moraes presided over Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial.Crime and insecurity were also top concerns for voters. Brazil's homicide rate has fallen, but street crime such as phone thefts, that are highly visible to voters, have increased - and violence and drug trafficking are still major problems.Bolsonaro has pledged to designate Brazilian gangs as terrorists and build maximum-security prisons akin to those in El Salvador. His father, during his presidency, loosened gun ownership restrictions.Lula has criticised the US terrorist designation of Brazilian gangs but launched various reforms to tackle the financial networks of organised crime networks, improve homicide investigations, and invest in prisons.The economy has also been central to this campaign: the country has high levels of personal debt and slowing growth.Lula has defined his legacy through a series of social welfare programmes, most notably Bolsa Família, that pays families to ensure children stay in education and receive healthcare such as vaccines, as well as building more universities. The programmes have been credited with lifting millions of Brazilians out of poverty.He has also backed oil drilling exploration, which has proved controversial with environmentalists, but he has a record of tightening environmental protections and reducing the rate of deforestation in the Amazon. Deforestation increased significantly under Jair Bolsonaro's presidency.Flávio Bolsonaro has pledged a public debt ceiling and government spending cuts, a revision of social welfare, and to bolster the critical minerals sector.

schema.headline: Brazil election goes to run-off as right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro wins first round

title: France braces for national day of student protests after injuries and mass arrests
description: France is braced for major protests on Tuesday, after organisers called for a nationwide day of action in support of students demanding more investmen
body: France is braced for major protests on Tuesday, after organisers called for a nationwide day of action in support of students demanding more investment in education.It comes after a week of demonstrations, which saw students blockading hundreds of schools, at least 190 students injured, and more than 5,000 people arrested.One student had his hand blown off during a confrontation on Monday, while another was reportedly struck in the head by a tear gas grenade last week.France's prime minister said the government had announced measures to address their demands, but the Union Syndicale Lycéenne (USL), a major organiser of the protests, said the government had offered "nothing concrete".The organisation called on people to join their mobilisation on Tuesday in the face of "this political deadlock and what we describe as unprecedented repression of the movement".Some other organisations have also shown their support for the students, with the teachers' union SNES-FSU urging its members to join Tuesday's protest.The radical-left La France Insoumise (LFI) party leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon described the protests as the "most powerful high school and university student youth movement" since 1968 - a year of major unrest, which saw millions of workers go on strike.The wave of demonstrations began in September in Paris and has spread across the country, with students protesting over a range of issues, including overcrowded classrooms, run-down buildings, and a lack of teachers.The protests were started by high school students, who were later joined by university students. Last week, Eden, 14, was badly hurt in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône after reportedly being struck on the head by a tear gas grenade. The student suffered "a double jaw fracture" and had to undergo "extremely major surgery", according to his lawyer.Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Eden's mother said her heart was "shattered"."It's shameful, it's appalling, it's violent, it's horrific," French media outlet BFMTV reported her as saying."This should not happen. They are dealing with children who are asking for better conditions in which to study."Among the 5,060 people arrested since the start of the movement, 87% were minors and 13% were adults, according to France's justice ministry, external. Fourteen people have reportedly been placed in pre-trial detention, while 1,802 people are facing prosecution, including 319 adults and 1,483 minors.The USL has accused police of using excessive force against the protesters. Responding to this allegation last week, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the demonstrations had been policed in "an extremely proportionate manner".While France's next presidential election is still months away, the protests and the response by French authorities have been heavily politicised.The government and hard-right politicians have blamed the hard left for fuelling the protests. Lecornu said LFI was being "irresponsible" in calling for the movement to expand.The leader of the hard-right National Rally, Marine Le Pen, has also criticised the left for its response."This is no longer about high school student protests. It is about riots organised by professionals and overseen by deputies from La France Insoumise," she said, calling for a new anti-rioting law to be passed.Meanwhile Mélenchon, the LFI's party's presidential candidate, has been blaming the police for "abuses of power", calling on people to take to the streets to "protect the youth demonstrations".The left-wing mayor of Marseille, Benoît Payan, condemned the "unacceptable violence" in his city. While young people were "legitimately concerned" about their future and public services, they must express themselves calmly, he said.

schema.headline: France braces for national day of student protests after injuries and mass arrests
